hpi_details: 24F graduate student presents requesting the HPV vaccine. She received one dose of the HPV vaccine at age 15 through the national immunisation programme but did not complete the series. She is currently sexually active with one male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago, and her next period is due soon. She has never had a cervical cancer screening (Pap test).
ideas: thinks she needs to restart the entire HPV vaccine series from the beginning because it has been so long since her first dose
concerns: worried that missing the remaining doses has left her completely unprotected against cervical cancer and HPV
expectations: wants to get the first shot of the restarted HPV vaccine series today
pmh: No chronic medical conditions. Received one dose of HPV vaccine at age 15.
social_hx: Graduate student. Sexually active with one male partner. Uses condoms inconsistently. Non-smoker, occasional alcohol use.

boundaries_and_exceptions: While HPV vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy, if administered inadvertently, no intervention is needed, but remaining doses should be delayed until after pregnancy.
Catch-up vaccination is generally recommended for all females up to age 26, and based on shared clinical decision-making for adults aged 27 to 45.
common_misconceptions: Recommending restarting the HPV vaccine series instead of just completing the remaining doses.
Administering the vaccine immediately without checking the possibility of current pregnancy.
Failing to advise the patient that vaccination does not replace the need for routine cervical screening.
Assuming that a patient who is already sexually active cannot benefit from the remaining HPV vaccine doses.
core_concepts: Patients with an interrupted HPV vaccination schedule do not need to restart the series; they should simply receive the remaining doses.
Pregnancy should be excluded before administering the HPV vaccine, and vaccination should be deferred if the patient is pregnant.
HPV vaccination does not treat existing HPV infections or HPV-associated lesions.
Vaccination does not replace the need for routine cervical cancer screening, which is recommended from age 20 in South Korea.
dangerous_errors: Administering the HPV vaccine to a potentially pregnant patient without verifying pregnancy status.
Missing the opportunity to initiate cervical cancer screening in a 24-year-old patient.
Failing to discuss contraception and safe sex practices in a sexually active young adult with inconsistent condom use.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: request for HPV vaccine catch-up
Key HPI features: 24F who received one HPV vaccine dose at age 15. Sexually active with inconsistent condom use. LMP 3 weeks ago. No prior Pap test.
Objective/Exam findings: Normal vital signs. Well-appearing female.
Relevant background/PMH: No chronic conditions. Incomplete vaccination history.
management_principles: Assess pregnancy status based on LMP and sexual history; perform a urine pregnancy test if pregnancy cannot be reliably excluded.
Administer the remaining doses of the HPV vaccine series (do not restart the series).
Initiate cervical cancer screening (cervical cytology/Pap test) as recommended from age 20 in South Korea.
Provide counselling on contraception and sexually transmitted infection (STI) prevention, emphasizing consistent condom use.

clinical_knowledge.topic: HPV catch-up vaccination and cervical cancer screening counselling

reference_soap.assessment: 1. Incomplete HPV vaccination status. 2. Need for cervical cancer screening. 3. Risk of unintended pregnancy and STIs due to inconsistent condom use.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 110/70, HR 72, Temp 36.8C, RR 14. Well-appearing female in no acute distress. General physical exam is unremarkable.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Obtain a urine pregnancy test today to exclude pregnancy before administering the HPV vaccine, given her LMP was 3 weeks ago and she has unprotected intercourse. 2. If not pregnant, administer the next dose of the HPV vaccine today to continue the series (no need to restart). 3. Schedule and perform a Pap smear for cervical cancer screening, as it is recommended starting at age 20 in Korea. 4. Counselled on the importance of consistent condom use for STI prevention and discussed reliable contraceptive options.
reference_soap.subjective: 24-year-old female graduate student presents to request the HPV vaccine. She received one dose at age 15 but never completed the series. She is sexually active with one male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. She has never had a Pap smear.

learning_objectives: Determine the appropriate catch-up schedule for a patient with an interrupted HPV vaccination series (continue, do not restart).
Identify the need to exclude pregnancy before administering the HPV vaccine in women of childbearing age.
Recognize the indications and age requirements for initiating routine cervical cancer screening (age 20 in South Korea).
Deliver effective counselling regarding safe sex practices, contraception, and the limitations of the HPV vaccine.

teaching.diagnosis: Incomplete HPV vaccination and health maintenance
differentials: Cervical dysplasia or current HPV infection

must_ask.say: Can you tell me more about the HPV vaccine you received when you were 15?
Are you currently sexually active, and do you use any form of protection?
When was the first day of your last menstrual period?
Have you ever had a Pap smear or cervical cancer screening before?
What did you think we needed to do today regarding your missed vaccine doses?

teaching.one_liner: A young adult with an interrupted HPV vaccine series simply needs to complete the remaining doses, but only after excluding pregnancy and ensuring she understands that vaccination doesn't replace regular cervical screening.
red_flags: Administering the HPV vaccine without confirming pregnancy status in a sexually active female with inconsistent contraception.
Neglecting to initiate cervical cancer screening in an eligible patient.

history.answer: I came in because I want to get the cervical cancer vaccine. I only got one dose years ago, so I think I need to start over.
I was talking with some friends recently and realized I never finished the cervical cancer shots. I wanted to come in and get protected.
I had one shot when I was 15 through the school program, but I missed the remaining doses and never followed up.
I feel completely fine today. I don't have a fever, chills, cough, nausea, or any sickness at all.
I just had mild soreness in my upper arm for a day or two after that first shot. I never had hives, facial swelling, or trouble breathing.
No, I do not have any allergies to eggs, gelatin, antibiotics, latex, or anything else that I know of.
No, I don't have any immune problems, and I've never taken steroids or immunosuppressive medications.
No, I have never received a blood transfusion or any immunoglobulin shots.
No, I have never had seizures, epilepsy, or any nerve conditions like Guillain-Barre syndrome.
No, I don't have any bleeding disorders, easy bruising, or take blood thinners.
No, I don't have any chronic illnesses like asthma, heart trouble, kidney disease, liver disease, or diabetes.
I am a graduate student studying literature. I don't work in healthcare or daycare, and I don't have any international travel planned.
I live by myself in a small apartment near my campus. No babies, pregnant women, or immunocompromised individuals live with me.
Since it has been almost nine years since that first shot, I assumed the vaccine has completely worn off and I need to start from dose one again.
I worry that because I never finished the series, I've been left completely unprotected against HPV and cervical cancer all this time.
I was hoping to get the first injection of the restarted series today if that is possible.
My last menstrual period started about three weeks ago, and my next one should be due in roughly a week. My cycle is very regular, every 28 days.
I am sexually active with my boyfriend. We try to use condoms, but we're not very consistent with them and don't use any other birth control.
I don't think I am pregnant, but since we didn't always use condoms, I suppose there is a slight chance. I'm completely fine with taking a urine test today.
I have one steady male partner right now. We've been together for about a year.
No, I have never had unusual vaginal discharge, foul odor, pelvic pain, or sores down there.
No, I have never had a Pap smear or any kind of cervical cancer screening test done.
I have no chronic medical conditions, and I have never been hospitalized or had surgery.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
No, I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes. I drink one or two glasses of beer socially on weekends, but not heavily.
There is no family history of cervical cancer, other cancers, or early chronic diseases in my family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-appearing young female in no acute distress with normal hydration and unlaboured breathing.
Bilateral deltoid areas are clean and intact without erythema, rash, swelling, or skin lesions.
Posterior oropharynx is clear without erythema, tonsillar enlargement, or exudates.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles.
Regular heart rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender in all four quadrants without guarding or rebound tenderness.
